advisory_lock_cancellation_deadlock_2026.headline: ROOT CAUSE OF THE SIBLING CANCELLATION HANG, established from LIVE PostgreSQL evidence, not inference: a pg_advisory_xact_lock is held across an in-process await, so cancellation queues behind the very work it is cancelling.
advisory_lock_cancellation_deadlock_2026.how_it_was_established: The test was run while sampling pg_stat_activity and pg_blocking_pids during the hang window. This replaced two earlier hypotheses that were both WRONG and are recorded as refuted below.

observed_blocking_chain.88652: wait_event = Client/ClientRead, blocked_by = {} -- THE HOLDER. Its last statement is `SELECT pg_advisory_xact_lock(hashtextextended($1, 0))`, so it took the advisory lock and then went IDLE IN TRANSACTION waiting on the application. It is not waiting on PostgreSQL at all; it is parked awaiting Rust.

advisory_lock_cancellation_deadlock_2026.mechanism: swarm_orchestration/routing_execution.rs defines `lock_execution` (line 2554) which issues pg_advisory_xact_lock(hashtextextended(execution_id, 0)) INSIDE a transaction, and it is called from EIGHT sites (lines 345, 369, 507, 716, 1256, 1822, 1982, 2221) including claim_ready (709) and record_generated_output (1566). Because the lock is an XACT lock it is held until that transaction ends. When a stage is mid-generation the holding transaction stays open across the generation await, and cancel_routing_execution - which needs the same execution-keyed advisory lock to terminalize - blocks behind it indefinitely. The advisory lock serializes on execution_id, so a slow or blocked stage makes the operator's cancel unreachable by construction.
advisory_lock_cancellation_deadlock_2026.why_the_other_symptom_differed: ac9_cancel_and_peer_failure_propagate_into_blocked_factory_create used hold_create, so the stall was in factory create BEFORE any generation transaction existed; bounding the post-cancel create wait (the fix already landed) resolved it and that test now passes. ac9_cancel_terminalizes_parallel_siblings_and_live_sessions uses hold_generation instead: both creates COMPLETE, the sessions are live, and the stall is inside generation while a routing transaction holds the advisory lock. Same visible symptom, genuinely different cause - which is why the first fix correctly did not mask the second.
hypotheses_raised_and_REFUTED: REFUTED: 'terminate() never fires the session cancel token, so generation never stops.' It does - coordinator.rs:4645 calls handle.cancel.cancel(), and the fixture's generate() stream polls cancel.is_cancelled() every 25ms and emits ModelRuntimeError::Cancelled.
REFUTED: 'the session teardown await is unbounded.' It is already bounded by config.teardown_timeout at coordinator.rs:4902 (5s default).

REFUTED (earlier, separately): 'the ledger writer STOP identity hardening broke external reclaim.' ProcessReclaim::reclaim_stop derives its STOP identity from the persisted row, so it stays byte-identical.
advisory_lock_cancellation_deadlock_2026.fix_shape_NOT_applied: The advisory lock must not span a model-generation await. Options: (a) take the lock, perform the state transition, COMMIT, and re-acquire for the post-generation write, so the lock is held only for the duration of a durable transition rather than the duration of inference; or (b) give cancellation a lock-free terminalization path so an operator cancel never queues behind stage work. Not applied here because it changes transactional boundaries on the routing terminal path - the exact class of change that produced three regressions earlier in this session when landed without full-suite validation, and the full mixed suite plus swarm suites are hours of runtime.
advisory_lock_cancellation_deadlock_2026.severity: Operator-facing. Any cancel of a routing execution whose stage is mid-generation will block for the duration of that generation. With a real model rather than a test fixture that is a long, unexplained UI stall on the cancel path.

transaction_across_generation_root_cause.headline: CORRECTED ROOT CAUSE. The advisory lock was a SYMPTOM. The actual defect is that the routing wave holds a PostgreSQL transaction OPEN ACROSS MODEL GENERATION, so every concurrent operation - including operator cancellation - queues behind inference.

transaction_across_generation_root_cause.what_this_means: A transaction that has read lane rows stays open for the entire duration of model inference. Any writer touching those rows blocks on the row lock, and anything needing the execution advisory lock then queues behind that writer. Cancellation is simply the first operation an operator notices, because it is the one they issue while inference is still running.
transaction_across_generation_root_cause.severity: Architectural and operator-facing. With a real model - not a fixture - inference can run for many seconds to minutes. For that whole window the routing execution's rows are transactionally pinned. This is a scalability and responsiveness defect well beyond the cancellation path.

cancellation_deadlock_ROOT_CAUSE_PROVEN_.why_this_is_conclusive: task36 appears twice: once holding on connection 87600 and once waiting on connection 83352. One logical operation therefore holds this key on one pooled connection while requesting it on another. PostgreSQL can never grant the second request, and the task can never reach the code that would release the first, because it is suspended awaiting that grant. This is a closed cycle inside a single task - not cross-task lock ordering, and not resource starvation.
cancellation_deadlock_ROOT_CAUSE_PROVEN_.why_every_earlier_theory_failed_to_fix_i: Each earlier theory attacked a DIFFERENT layer and therefore could not work: raising max_connections 5 -> 25 only lets the same task grab another connection and self-block sooner (measured: hang got WORSE, 318.1s); the multi_thread runtime experiment could not help because the cycle is within one task regardless of worker-thread count; and 'commit before awaiting inference' does not apply because the lock is not held across inference at all.
cancellation_deadlock_ROOT_CAUSE_PROVEN_.mechanism_traced_in_code: coordinator.rs::dispatch_ready_routing_stages drives every stage future in ONE FuturesUnordered inside a single spawned worker task, then consumes it with `while let Some(result) = pending.next().await`. A stage future can be suspended mid-transaction while still holding lock_execution (the transaction, and therefore the xact-scoped advisory lock, survives the suspension). The consumer loop - running in that SAME task - then calls cancel_active_routing_siblings on a failed/cancelled dispatch, which reaches routing_execution.rs::cancel_execution (lock_execution at line 2289) and requests the same execution key. The suspended stage future can only resume once the consumer's await completes, and the consumer's await can only complete once the suspended future releases the lock. Deadlock.
cancellation_deadlock_ROOT_CAUSE_PROVEN_.lock_sites_mapped: routing_execution.rs lock_execution callers by line: 345 snapshot, 437 diagnostics_for_run, 575 begin_execution, 784 claim_ready, 1324 record_stage_result_tx, 1890 record_generated_output, 2050 recover_expired_claims, 2289 cancel_execution. The stage path reaches 1324 via record_transition/heartbeat_claim; the consumer path reaches 2289 via cancel_active_routing_siblings.

cancellation_deadlock_ROOT_CAUSE_PROVEN_.fix_shape: Break the cycle rather than widen the lock. Either (a) the consumer loop must not request the execution advisory lock while any stage future it drives may still hold it - drain/settle the in-flight futures first, or move sibling cancellation out of the same task; or (b) cancel_execution and the stage terminal transition must share ONE transaction/lock acquisition passed down, instead of each opening its own. Widening the pool, changing runtime flavor, or reordering inference are all proven not to help.

cancellation_defects_RESOLVED_idempotent.the_real_defect: Two legitimate actors race to terminalize the same session - coordinator.rs::cancel_routing_execution (the operator's cancel) and the worker's stage-failure path, which fires BECAUSE that cancellation stopped the stream. terminate() rejected any second request whose intent differed, which made CONCURRENT terminalization impossible. That is the wrong invariant for a swarm coordinator: an ordinary race became a hard failure.
cancellation_defects_RESOLVED_idempotent.why_ordering_could_never_fix_it: Measured both ways. Teardown-first: the worker terminalizes the execution as Failed and cancel_execution's terminal guard refuses -> operator's cancel is not the recorded outcome (AC-9 unsatisfiable). Persist-first: the worker records its cleanup intent first and the operator's cancel_session is rejected as a mismatched retry. Ordering only selects which actor loses, which is why fix attempt 2 regressed rather than helped.

The FIRST durable intent stays authoritative and its owner still performs the teardown and writes the terminal receipt, so nothing is swallowed and no orphan is hidden. A genuine retry (same intent, no owner currently running) still falls through to the ownership-generation bump unchanged.

Any number of requesters may ask for termination; exactly one owns it.

teardowns_orphan_defect_DIAGNOSED_2026_0.headline: DIAGNOSED (not yet fixed): teardowns==1 happens because coordinator.rs::terminate() gates the RUNTIME TEARDOWN behind two durable writes that can return Err first. A failed database write therefore leaves a live session running.
call_order_in_terminate: 1. fence the live handle (fire the cancel token) - no teardown yet
3. record_lane_terminal_status(...).await - EARLY RETURN on Err ('Dexterity terminal lane state record failed')
4. gather handle fields, cancel token + runtime.cancel
5. run_teardown_bounded(instance_id, teardown) - THE ONLY STEP THAT TEARS THE SESSION DOWN
teardowns_orphan_defect_DIAGNOSED_2026_0.why_that_produces_the_symptom: The test's teardown counter is incremented by the SessionTeardown closure, which is only invoked from run_teardown_bounded at step 5. If either durable write at step 2 or 3 fails for one of the two sessions, terminate() returns before step 5 and that session is never torn down - teardowns==1 instead of 2, with a live session left behind.
teardowns_orphan_defect_DIAGNOSED_2026_0.why_this_is_a_real_product_defect_not_a_: It means a PostgreSQL/EventLedger write failure orphans a running model session. That is an HBR-QUIET-003 process-ownership violation, and it contradicts the reasoning this same coordinator already applies elsewhere (the bounded factory-create wait argues explicitly that an orphaned process is recoverable via process-ledger reclaim while an unrecoverable state is not). Runtime teardown must not be gated behind durable-write success.
teardowns_orphan_defect_DIAGNOSED_2026_0.recommended_fix: Make runtime teardown unconditional: perform the teardown (and the runtime cancel) regardless of whether the durable writes succeeded, capture any durable-write error, and return it AFTER teardown has run. That preserves the error report while guaranteeing no orphan. Do not simply reorder the writes after teardown without capturing their errors, or a failed receipt becomes silent.
teardowns_orphan_defect_DIAGNOSED_2026_0.explicitly_NOT_caused_by_the_2026_08_05_: teardowns==1 was recorded on 2026-08-05 in 3 of the original 11 runs, before any change in this session. It persists at 2 of 6 after the cancellation fixes at a similar rate. The lock_timeout bound, the idempotent terminalization and the persist-first ordering neither introduced nor masked it.
teardowns_orphan_defect_DIAGNOSED_2026_0.status_unchanged: No lifecycle status changed. Not fixed; diagnosis only, so that the next actor starts from the mechanism rather than re-deriving it.

FIX APPLIED (errors deferred, teardown runs first, first error returned at the normal exit). Rate did not move (2/6 -> 2/8).
